books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: William Graham Sumner, What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883)
Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, January 1891
Jane Addams, “The Subjective Necessity for Social Settlements,” in Philanthropy and Social Progress (1893)
Carl Schurz, “Restricting Immigration,” Harper's Weekly, January 8, 1898

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which responses to immigration changed the United States between 1865 and 1898.

documents.title: Congress suspends Chinese labor immigration
documents.source: Chinese Exclusion Act, May 6, 1882 (22 Stat. 58), Section 1 and preamble. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The law itself; shows Congress banning entry by nationality for the first time.
documents.text:
“Whereas in the opinion of the Government of the United States the coming of Chinese laborers to this country endangers the good order of certain localities within the territory thereof: Therefore, Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That from and after the expiration of ninety days next after the passage of this act, and until the expiration of ten years next after the passage of this act, the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended; and during such suspension it shall not be lawful for any Chinese laborer to come, or having so come after the expiration of said ninety days to remain within the United States.”

Chinese Exclusion Act, approved May 6, 1882.

documents.title: Sumner on survival of the fittest
documents.source: William Graham Sumner, What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Yale sociologist's argument; shows an idea that justified leaving the poor unaided.
documents.text: “The struggle for existence is aimed against nature. . . . Competition, therefore, is a law of nature. Nature is entirely neutral; she submits to him who most energetically and resolutely assails her. She grants her rewards to the fittest, therefore, without regard to other considerations of any kind. . . . Let it be understood that we cannot go outside of this alternative: liberty, inequality, survival of the fittest; not-liberty, equality, survival of the unfittest.”

documents.title: Lodge demands restriction
documents.source: Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, vol. 152 (January 1891), p. 32. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A congressman's case for restriction; shows nativism framed as a judgment on race and literacy.
documents.text: “Thus it is proved, first, that immigration to this country is increasing, and, second, that it is making its greatest relative increase from races most alien to the body of the American people and from the lowest and most illiterate classes among those races. In other words, it is apparent that, while our immigration is increasing, it is showing at the same time a marked tendency to deteriorate in character.”

documents.title: The Immigration Restriction League
documents.source: Paraphrased from the founding statement of the Immigration Restriction League, Boston, 1894.
documents.sourcing: Nativists' own program; shows restriction moving from one group to all new immigrants.
documents.text: Paraphrased from the League's founding statement: the League called for a literacy test for all arriving immigrants, arguing that the flood of illiterate newcomers from southern and eastern Europe threatened American institutions and that only a reading test could keep out those unfit for citizenship.

documents.title: Immigration by decade
documents.source: U.S. Immigration Commission, 1911, Table 2, “Immigration to the United States, 1820 to 1910, by Decade,” compiled from official sources. Public data.
documents.sourcing: Immigration counts; shows the 1880s surge that fed the nativist response.

documents.title: Addams on the settlement
documents.source: Jane Addams, “The Subjective Necessity for Social Settlements,” in Philanthropy and Social Progress (1893). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A settlement founder's own account; shows reformers answering immigration with aid, not exclusion.
documents.text: “The Settlement, then, is an experimental effort to aid in the solution of the social and industrial problems which are engendered by the modern conditions of life in a great city. . . . It must be hospitable and ready for experiment.”

documents.title: Schurz answers the literacy test
documents.source: Carl Schurz, “Restricting Immigration,” Harper's Weekly, January 8, 1898. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A critic of restriction writing for a general magazine; shows the literacy test opposed on its own terms.
documents.text: “No educational test is needed to that end. Nor will any educational test keep out unknown anarchists or other dangerous characters, for such persons are sure to be able to read and write twenty words of our Constitution in one language or more. . . . It is more than grotesque to exclude by law persons with two strong arms and an honest willingness to work because they are unable to read and write twenty words of the Federal Constitution.”

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a thesis that makes a historically defensible claim about the extent to which responses to immigration changed the United States between 1865 and 1898, with a line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: A thesis that merely restates the prompt, or one that makes no claim about extent, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as post-Civil War industrialization, the growth of cities, or the rise of mass immigration.
rubric.notEarned: A context that is only background on one document, or one set outside the period, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using the content of at least three documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least six documents to support the argument, with specific evidence from each.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least one piece of specific outside evidence, such as the opening of Ellis Island in 1892, the Alien Contract Labor Law of 1885, or the settlement house movement, to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating document content without adding outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for explaining how at least one document’s point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience matters to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying a document’s author without explaining why that matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a complex argument, such as showing that restriction changed the law while aid changed the cities, or that the same arrivals were welcomed as workers and feared as strangers.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument that ignores counter-evidence, or a complexity move stated without support, does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 responses to immigration changed the United States to a large extent, writing exclusion into federal law for the first time and building a new reform movement in the cities, although the change stopped short of shutting the door, since immigration kept growing.
Context: The Civil War ended with factories, railroads, and mines growing fast, and the 1880s brought the largest immigration wave yet, mostly from southern and eastern Europe, on top of older Irish, German, and Chinese arrivals.
Evidence: Document 5 shows the scale: immigration nearly doubled from 2,812,191 in 1871-1880 to 5,246,613 in 1881-1890. Document 1 shows the sharpest response: Congress suspended the entry of Chinese laborers for ten years. Document 3 shows restriction widening, with Lodge calling the new immigrants the lowest and most illiterate classes among those races.
Evidence continued: Document 4 shows the Immigration Restriction League demanding a literacy test for all newcomers. Document 2 shows the idea behind leaving the poor alone: Sumner called competition a law of nature that rewarded the fittest. Document 6 answers differently: Addams called the settlement an experimental effort to aid the city, and Document 7 shows Schurz mocking the literacy test as grotesque.
Outside evidence: Ellis Island opened in 1892 to process the new arrivals, and the Alien Contract Labor Law of 1885 had already barred employers from importing contract workers.
Complexity: restriction changed the law while settlement houses changed the cities, so the same immigration that filled the factories also divided Americans over what America should be.
